docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome to the official Leigh Hackspace Wiki, your guide to our community workspace.

This Wiki is designed to provide detailed instructions on how to make use of our diverse facilities and tools, give insight into key processes, and provide contact information for important individuals within the community.

This Wiki is a living, public resource, and we welcome your input. If you spot something that needs updating or improvement, feel free to contribute by accessing our GitHub repository, linked in the top right corner of this site. The wiki belongs to everyone, for everyone.

docs.title: Facilities
docs.text:
This section will give a quick overview of our facilities and the tools within.

Here is a quick floorplan view of the hackspace:

At the moment the main entrance to the hackspace is via the Pi Room. Most rooms will be locked unless being actively used, and its suggested that you pop in to the Pi Room to make yourself known.

docs.title: Artist Pods
docs.text:
Our Artist Pods offer individual, partitioned spaces for lease by makers and artists looking for a dedicated area to create and innovate. Conveniently located in an open area, the pods share proximity with the Fabrication, Workshop, and the Crafts Space, offering easy access to a range of resources.

Interested in a personal creative space within Leigh Hackspace? Feel free to reach out to one of our directors for further information on renting an Artist Pod.

docs.title: Classroom
docs.text: Our Hackspace features a classroom designed to accommodate 6-8 people. This is ideal for small-group instruction, discussion, and collaborative learning.

docs.title: Dark Room
docs.text: Our Dark Room provides a specially controlled environment for those passionate about traditional photography. It's your go-to space for developing and processing photographic film, allowing you to delve into the intricate world of analog imagery.

docs.title: Electronics
docs.text: Our Electronics Bench, situated in the main space, is your dedicated space for soldering and managing those mischievous circuits. This area boasts an abundant supply of parts and a variety of tools designed to support you in bringing your electronic projects to life.

docs.title: Main Space
docs.text:
Our Main Space serves as the heart of Leigh Hackspace, providing the most generous area for general use, and currently housing our dedicated Electronics zone.

Please note that the layout and usage of the Main Space is currently in a state of flux. Currently, it is functioning as our primary storage area, temporarily housing various items until we designate more suitable locations. We appreciate your understanding as we work to enhance the space.

docs.title: Pi Room
docs.text: Our Pi Room serves as a versatile space, equipped with desks and PCs ready for member use. It's an ideal location for collaborative work, or as a meeting hub for technical events.

docs.title: 3D Printers
docs.text:
We have 3 printers available for all members to use after training.

All printers are networked, and we ask that you use the linked OctoPrint server when printing your files.

CAD-1 is available for you to design, slice and print your models. PrusaSlicer is pre-configured for all the printers.

If you want to use PrusaSlicer on your own system then the profiles are linked below for each printer. If you're only going to use the hackspace's printers you can save time and download a packaged version of CAD-1's configuration to use on your own system.

You are responsible for ensuring the safe operation of printers. Do not leave the printers unattended for prolonged periods of time. If you are in doubt about the operation of the printers, please ask, and someone will be happy to help.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
There's a number of repeatable steps to printing on our printers. We're hoping that everyone can follow them and have a consistent experience.

  • You'll need a STL model file to print. Find one online, or design your own using the CAD tools available.
  • If using CAD-1, PrusaSlicer is configured for the printers.
  • If not using CAD-1, download PrusaSlicer and the PrusaSlicer profile for the printer you want to use.
  • Copy the profile files to your local Prusa folder (c:\users\USERNAME\AppData\Roaming\PrusaSlicer on Windows).
  • Start PrusaSlicer, import your STL.
  • Slice your model and export a GCode file.
  • Open the OctoPrint for your printer, and login (ask if you don't have the password).
  • Drag the sliced GCode file to the OctoPrint server.
  • Turn on the printer.
  • Ensure filament is loaded.
  • Click on the file in OctoPrint to load, print your file from OctoPrint.
  • Keep an eye on OctoPrint and the printer as your file is printing.

Our printers:

docs.title: Lasers
docs.text:
We have 1 laser engraver/cutter available for all members to use after training.

The laser engraver is networked, and we ask that you use the linked LaserWeb server when running your files.

You are responsible for ensuring the safe operation of lasers. Do not leave lasers unattended. Do not operate lasers without the safety cover in place. If you are in doubt about the operation of lasers, please ask, and someone will be happy to help.

Workflow:

There's a number of repeatable steps to engraving/cutting on our lasers. We're hoping that everyone can follow them and have a consistent experience.

  • You will need a SVG or PNG/JPG to upload to cut/engrave.
  • Open LaserWeb for the Laser.
  • Turn on the laser cutter.
  • Drag your image in to LaserWeb, resize and place in the bottom left of the laser bed.
  • Set tool paths for the parts of your image. See the settings for the laser.
  • Connect to the laser, clear any errors, and nudge the printer to the bottom left corner. Take care to not hit the frame.
  • When you are over the bottom left corner, set 0,0.
  • Nudge the head far enough away to place your work piece.
  • Important close the laser shield.
  • Start the laser. Do not open until the work is complete. If a problem occurs, cancel in LaserWeb.
  • Nudge the head to allow you to remove your piece.

docs.title: Vinyl Cutters
docs.text:
We have 1 vinyl cutter availble for all members to use.

The vinyl cutter is attached to CAD-1, and works with InkCut. Inkcut will cut your SVG designs.

Workflow:

  • Transfer your SVG file to CAD-1.
  • Turn on the vinyl cutter.
  • Open Inkcut, and load your SVG file.
  • Check the dimensions of your SVG file.
  • Load vinyl in to the vinyl cutter. If error is displayed, the lever is probably up.
  • Blade pressure is imporant. See the section on test cuts and pressure.
  • Send file to printer.

Test Cuts and Pressure:

  • The pressure should be pre-set for thin vinyl.
  • When first coming to the printer and printing with a new sheets, it's imporant to perform a test cut before cutting your own design.
  • Start with the lightest pressure, and add more pressure until you make a good cut. Add no more pressure.

docs.text: The social space is a great place to host small user groups and events, with plenty of seating, desks, and a small food/drink service area.

docs.text:

docs.title: On The Day
docs.text:
On the day of the event, arrive at least an hour before to allow yourself time to setup anything needed in the social space. A keyholder will meet you to open up the space, and depending on the time and schedule may be able to stay with you until your event is over.

The opening and closing the social space is the responsibility of the key holder, but the event organiser is responsible for returning the social space back to the condition it was in before the event.

After the event has finished, please notify the keyholder. How will vary person to person and needs to be discussed with the keyholder.

  • Use a diamond file to treat the tool's sharp edges.
  • If the tool has a nick or dent in the cutting edge, then treat the tool on the bench grinder.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text: This section will cover any details of the hackspace's technical infrastructure, that being things that have blinking lights and beepity boops.

docs.title: The Shape Of It
docs.text:
Everything comes in through one box, gw, which is the router, firewall, DHCP server, DNS server, VPN endpoint, and the TLS front door for every service we publish. Behind it are four NixOS machines (services1, services2, services3, aibox), a TrueNAS box for storage and backups, a Proxmox host for the VMs that don't fit the NixOS fleet, and three ProCurve switches.

Single sign-on across all of it is Authentik at id.leighhack.org. If you have an account there you can reach the internal dashboards, the tailnet VPN, the switches, and the member VMs.

docs.title: Configuration Is In Git
docs.text:
The servers and the network are defined in leigh-hackspace/infrastructure-nix-flake and deployed with nixos-rebuild switch. That includes the bits that used to live in a web UI: DNS records, DHCP reservations, firewall rules, the VLANs, every vhost, and each service's config. So for most of the network there is nothing to log into and click - the change is a commit, and machines/ and common/ in that repo are the real reference.

Each page here says which file owns what it describes. When a page and the repo disagree, the repo is right.

docs.title: Internal Services
docs.text:
The hackspace runs a collection of services on the hackspace network, either to assist with automation or just to be useful for members.

Everything is HTTPS and everything is behind the front door on the router, so a *.int.leighhack.org name resolves on the space's networks and on the tailnet only. Names without .int are public. Most of them want you to be signed in with your id.leighhack.org account.

Service Address Reachable from Monitoring overview status.leighhack.org Anywhere, once signed in Prometheus prometheus.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN, Infra Grafana grafana.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN, Infra Gatus (uptime alerts) gatus.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN Router/network dashboard network-info.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN Switch management switch.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN, Infra Proxmox monster.int.leighhack.org Anywhere, Members read / Infra write TrueNAS truenas.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN, Infra Authentik id.leighhack.org Anywhere UniFi (access points) unifi-admin.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN, Infra Home Assistant ha.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN Frigate (cameras) frigate.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN zigbee2mqtt zigbee2mqtt.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN Filestore filestore.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN, Infra Membership (GoCardless) dashboard gocardless.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN, Directors + Infra Speedtest speed.leighhack.org Anywhere Photos (Immich) immich.leighhack.org Anywhere Matrix / Element matrix.leighhack.org, element.leighhack.org Anywhere Mattermost mattermost.leighhack.org Anywhere Outline (wiki) outline.leighhack.org Anywhere Audiobooks (Alexandria) alexandria.int.leighhack.org LAN / VPN Inference API strata.leighhack.org Anyone with the API key Space status feed api.leighhack.org Anywhere

Each one is a row in common/front-door.nix in the infra repo, and that table is what the router's nginx is generated from - which is why a name either has a row or doesn't resolve. "LAN / VPN" means the row is answered only to the space's own address ranges and the tailnet; "Anywhere" means it isn't. Some of those also want a sign-in at the door before they'll answer - that's the sso flag on the row, and it's Authentik doing the checking. "Infra"/"Members" means the application itself applies a group check on top.

docs.title: Printers
docs.text:
The member printer is a Brother MFC-L3740CDW colour laser MFP, at 10.3.2.30 / brother.int.leighhack.org. It's on the wireless VLAN and advertises itself over mDNS, so any device that supports IPP/AirPrint should find it; the raw IPP queue is ipp://10.3.2.30/ipp/print.

The old HP Laserjet and the Epson inkjet in the Pi Room are gone - the Brother is the only printer answering on the network. If you can't find it, or need something printed and can't work out how, contact infra.

docs.title: NAS Storage
docs.text:
Storage is a TrueNAS box - nas2.int.leighhack.org, 10.3.1.6, in Rack 1 - holding the member data, the camera recordings, and the Proxmox VM disks. It should give a reasonable amount of reliability, and we still provide no guarantees about data on it.

  • NFS is for the servers. Members don't need it.
  • SMB guest access is available for share access; there are no private CIFS shares.
  • Members who log in on the network (the Pi Room, aibox) get a home directory on it. Its ACL is your Authentik account, so the account is the backup of your identity here.

While it should be reliable, it is slow to come up after a power cut, and everything that needs it waits for it rather than failing. Ask infra if you have a specific requirement for a share.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
There are backups, of a sort: services1's /srv (its databases, its configs, the state of most of what's in the table above) is pushed to the NAS with borg on a schedule, and the borg server is a container on the NAS itself.

That means the NAS holds the only copy of everything, including itself. Anything that matters to you personally should exist somewhere else too. Nobody is checking restores on a rota - if that changes you'll see it here.

docs.title: Filestore
docs.text:
Filestore is a web file browser over the NAS filestore share, at filestore.int.leighhack.org. It's an Infra tool now - signed in with Authentik, gated to the Infra group - and it does thumbnailing, search, preview, and drag-and-drop upload.

It is not scanned for viruses. It used to be, and the scanner isn't wired in any more, so treat the share as unfiltered storage.

docs.title: Single Sign-On
docs.text: Everything above authenticates against Authentik at id.leighhack.org. Your membership subscription is what puts you in the Members group, and that group is what the tailnet and the general services check; Infra is what gets you into the administrative ones. Ask infra if you think you should be in one and aren't.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Prometheus scrapes every machine we control (and the print servers' APIs), Grafana draws it, and Gatus checks the endpoints and shouts in Slack when one stops answering. status.leighhack.org is the public view of that, and each box also runs its own little status dashboard (services1-status.int, services2-status.int, aibox-status.int) for when the monitoring itself is the thing that's broken.

If you want something scraped or checked, drop a message to infra.

docs.title: MQTT
docs.text: An MQTT broker is available at mqtt.int.leighhack.org, port 1883. It is still unauthenticated and there is no TLS listener, so anything on the network or the tailnet can read and publish whatever it likes - which is fine for the sensors and dashboards it's used for, and is not a channel for anything secret. Home Assistant, Frigate and zigbee2mqtt all dial it.

docs.title: Inference
docs.text:
We have three GPU/accelerated boxes offering OpenAI-compatible endpoints:

  • strata.leighhack.org - public, API key required (ask infra)
  • strata.int.leighhack.org and strata2.int.leighhack.org - the same engines on the LAN, where the door injects the key so local clients don't need one
  • llama.int.leighhack.org - llama.cpp on services3 (a GTX 1080 Ti), LAN only
  • whisper.int.leighhack.org - speech to text, over a WebSocket

The chat UI at ai.leighhack.org lives on aibox and shares that box with the build machine; when the big engine is loaded there isn't enough RAM for both, so the UI being down is usually "someone is running inference", not an outage.

docs.title: Cameras, Door, and Phones
docs.text:
Frigate is our NVR (frigate.int.leighhack.org) for the eight feeds around the space, plus a scene-change monitor that watches the main space. The door entry system has its own UI at doors.int.leighhack.org and an API at api-doors.int. The intercom is bare Asterisk on services1, answering 10.3.1.166, and the state switch by the front door is what sets whether we're open.

The Space API (/space.json, /events.ics) is the public, machine-readable version of that - whether we're open, and what's on.

Read the Proxmox page before you build anything important: the disks live on the NAS, there are no backups of any VM, and the host is a single machine.

docs.title: LBPT Tenant Network Agreement
docs.text:
LBPT Tenant Network Agreement

GDPR Policy for LBPT Tenant Internet Network

Revision 1.0

Effective Date: 17/7/2023

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text: This GDPR policy outlines the guidelines and responsibilities for tenants of Leigh Building Preservation Trust (LBPT) regarding the use of the internet network provided by LBPT. This policy aims to ensure the security and protection of personal data as required by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). All tenants accessing the LBPT network must comply with this policy.

docs.title: 2. Definitions
docs.text:
• LBPT: Leigh Building Preservation Trust
  • Tenant: Any individual or organization leasing or occupying a space within LBPT premises.
  • Network: The internet network provided by LBPT to tenants.

docs.title: 3. General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Compliance
docs.text: LBPT is committed to protecting the personal data of its tenants and ensuring compliance with GDPR regulations. Tenants are required to follow the guidelines outlined in this policy to ensure the security and privacy of personal data processed through the LBPT network.

docs.title: 4.1. Device Security
docs.text:
• 4.1.1. Tenants are responsible for ensuring the security of their own devices (computers, smartphones, tablets, etc.) used to access the LBPT network.
  • 4.1.2. Devices must have up-to-date security software (e.g., antivirus, firewall, anti-malware) installed and active at all times.
  • 4.1.3. Tenants should promptly address any security vulnerabilities or breaches detected on their devices and take appropriate action to mitigate and resolve them.

docs.title: 4.2. Software and Hardware Updates
docs.text:
• 4.2.1. Tenants must ensure that all software and hardware utilized to access the LBPT network are kept up to date with the latest security patches and updates.
  • 4.2.2. Regularly check for and apply updates to operating systems, applications, firmware, and other relevant software installed on devices used to connect to the LBPT network.
  • 4.2.3. Keep hardware devices (routers, modems, switches, etc.) updated with the latest firmware provided by the manufacturer.

docs.title: 4.3. User Authentication and Access Control
docs.text:
• 4.3.1. Tenants should use strong, unique passwords for their devices and accounts used to access the LBPT network.
  • 4.3.2. Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) whenever possible to add an extra layer of security to user accounts.
  • 4.3.3. Do not share login credentials with unauthorized individuals and take necessary precautions to prevent unauthorized access to devices or accounts.

docs.title: 5.1. Monitoring and Security Measures
docs.text:
• 5.1.1. LBPT will implement appropriate security measures to monitor and protect the network infrastructure against unauthorized access, malicious activities, and data breaches.
  • 5.1.2. LBPT may employ network monitoring tools to detect and respond to security incidents or potential threats. By using the network, tenants consent to the collection and processing of network traffic data for security purposes.

docs.title: 5.2. Data Protection and Privacy
docs.text:
• 5.2.1. LBPT will ensure that appropriate technical and organizational measures are in place to safeguard the personal data transmitted over the network in accordance with GDPR requirements.
  • 5.2.2. LBPT will not access or monitor the content of tenants' communications unless required to do so by law or necessary to protect the network's security and integrity.

docs.title: 6. Reporting Security Incidents
docs.text:
• 6.1. Tenants must promptly report any suspected or confirmed security incidents, data breaches, or unauthorized access to LBPT's network administrators.

  • 6.2. Report security incidents to the following contact:

  • data@imagevillage.co.uk

  • Mark Nightingale – Network Systems Administrator
  • Image Village | Floor 3.4 | Spinners Mill | Park Lane | Leigh | WN7 2LB

docs.title: 7. Policy Compliance and Enforcement
docs.text:
• 7.1. Non-compliance with this policy and/or the tenancy terms of service may result in sanctions, including temporary or permanent suspension of network access privileges, as determined by LBPT.
  • 7.2. LBPT reserves the right to amend this policy as required to reflect changes in technology, legal requirements, or business needs.

Tenants acknowledge that they have read, understood, and agree to comply with the tenants terms of service as outlined in section 4. Failure to comply may result in further actions, as outlined in section 7 of this policy.

Any tenant who disagrees with the terms outlined in this policy are NOT required to sign this document and understand non-compliance with these terms means LBPT will NOT provide access to their network, any existing network service(s) (if active) will be terminated immediately.

Tenants signing this document will be provided with our network services for the duration of their tenancy.

docs.title: Out of Band Access

docs.title: VPN
docs.text:
Leigh Hackspace offers a VPN service to its members, this allows you connect to hackspace internal services while outside of the space itself.

We run our own Tailscale network (the control server is Headscale, on the router), so you use the normal Tailscale client on Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, and iOS. It is not Tailscale's hosted service: you tell the client to use our coordination server, and you sign in with id.leighhack.org.

The old OpenVPN service is retired. It went away with the pfSense box it ran on; the configs at the bottom of this page are kept for the record and do not connect.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: You'll need an account on id.leighhack.org. Ideally, sign up with the same email address that you used for your GoCardless membership and privileges will be automatically assigned - that puts you in the Members group, which is what the VPN checks. If not, then contact Infra.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Install Tailscale, then point it at our server. On the command line:

sudo tailscale up --login-server=https://tailscale.leighhack.org

That prints a URL; open it, sign in with your Authentik account, and the device is on the network. Every device you've ever joined is listed in the admin UI at tailscale.leighhack.org/admin, so you can rename or remove old ones yourself.

The apps have the same option in their settings rather than on the command line - it's usually called "Use custom hosting provider" or "Self-hosted" (Android: the three-dot menu on the sign-in screen; iOS: Settings → Advanced). Put https://tailscale.leighhack.org in it, then sign in.

docs.title: Linux, GNOME, and Network Manager
docs.text: The GNOME Network VPN panel has no Tailscale support - Tailscale is not a protocol NetworkManager speaks, it's a program with its own daemon. So install the tailscale package for your distro, and then either run the command above or install the GNOME extension that wraps it. There's nothing to import and no profile to configure.

docs.title: Make sure you get the LAN
docs.text:
Subnet routes are offered by the router and approved by us, but a client has to say it will use them:

sudo tailscale set --accept-routes

Without it you'll reach the services that run on tailnet addresses and nothing else - a 10.3.1.20 or 10.3.14.61 connection will just time out, which looks like "the VPN is broken" and isn't.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
This VPN will give you access the same as being on the WiFi within the hackspace. All of 10.3.0.0/16, the 10.3.x.x VLANs, the CS network at 192.168.2.0/24, and the space's IPv6 are reachable, and with the tailnet's DNS turned on *.int.leighhack.org resolves and the short machine names work too.

The router also offers itself as an exit node, if you want everything on a device to come out of the space rather than just the traffic destined for us. Ask Infra to turn that on for your device.

If you have any specific requirements you need from the VPN then contact Infra.

docs.title: The Old OpenVPN Configs
docs.text:
These are the configs for the service we ran before the router was rebuilt. They will not connect: there is no OpenVPN server listening, and we haven't rebuilt one because the old one's keys and its Authentik bind account only existed on the retired appliance. If you genuinely need OpenVPN rather than Tailscale, say why to Infra.

  • VPN Configuration
  • VPN Configuration for older OpenVPN versions

docs.title: Devices
docs.text: The machines and gadgets we run, and how to do the administrative jobs on each one. Anything here that a server does is configured in the infrastructure repo; these pages are for the things you have to know rather than the things you have to type.

docs.title: Authentik
docs.text:
Authentik is the system we use to provide single sign-on and administration of users within the Hackspace.

https://id.leighhack.org/

It's the front door for everything in Internal Services, and it's also where your account lives for logging into the Pi Room machines and the servers. The Members group (put there by a nightly sync from your GoCardless membership) is what the tailnet and the member-facing services check; Infra is what gets you into the administrative ones.

docs.title: Where It Runs
docs.text:
Containers on services1 - server, worker, Postgres, Redis, and the RADIUS and LDAP outposts, all under podman, all managed by the infra repo. That moved here from a dedicated appliance VM on 2026-10-28.

authentik.int.leighhack.org and 10.3.1.36 are answered by that box, and 10.3.1.36 is a second address on services1, not a machine. It was kept as an address rather than moved because the ProCurve switches have radius-server host 10.3.1.36 in NVRAM and the LDAP clients point at the name; both groups are unreconfigurable. The old VM (108 on Proxmox) is stopped, has onboot cleared, and must stay that way - it still has the live DHCP reservation for that address, so starting it means two hosts answering one address.

Two things that are load-bearing and must not be "tidied up":

  • AUTHENTIK_SECRET_KEY is unrotatable. The database we migrated was sealed with it and Authentik cannot re-encrypt what it has already written. Rotating it locks the installation.
  • The outpost tokens (RADIUS and LDAP) live in the database and came across with it. Same argument.

docs.title: What It's Wired Into
docs.text:
• OIDC for our own apps (Grafana, Filestore, switch-gui, the membership dashboard, and the rest), always authorization-code with S256 PKCE and an Infra/Members group check
  • The tailnet - devices sign in with Authentik and only the Members group is allowed
  • RADIUS for the network switches, and LDAP/S for the Pi Room and anything else that wants a directory. Note the switches don't actually authenticate over RADIUS yet - see Network Switches
  • Unix accounts on the NixOS boxes: your uid is 2000 + your Authentik user id, and that number is the ACL on your NAS home directory. It is derived, not stored, so don't delete and re-create a user to fix something

docs.title: Reset a user's password
docs.text:
• Login to Authentik as a Administrator
  • Click on the "Admin interface" button in the top right
  • On the left menu, expand 'Directory' and select 'Users'
  • Select the user required
  • Click 'Reset password' and follow the form guide.

docs.title: Disable a user
docs.text:
Disabling a user will immediately stop them accessing most services, and also restrict access via the door system.

  • Login to Authentik as a Administrator
  • Click on the "Admin interface" button in the top right
  • On the left menu, expand 'Directory' and select 'Users'
  • Select the user required
  • Click 'Edit', untick the 'Is Active' field, and click Save.

docs.title: Add or remove someone from Infra
docs.text: Same route, 'Groups' instead of 'Users', then Infra → Members. This takes effect on a login rather than instantly: a session that's already signed in keeps whatever groups it was issued with until it re-authenticates.

docs.title: Create an OIDC app
docs.text:
Read docs/authentik-oidc-notes.md in the infra repo first. It has the provider table and three things that each cost someone a session: copy the flows and signing_key from a known-good provider rather than making new ones, duration fields must be key=value (minutes=5, never 5m - 5m saves fine and then 500s at the authorize endpoint), and a custom scope needs a real ScopeMapping child row, because a plain PropertyMapping is silently ignored.

Client secrets are write-only in the UI but readable through the ORM, so never dump a whole provider object into a terminal, a log, or a screenshot.

docs.title: Scripting against it
docs.text:
The admin REST API can't be used from the box it runs on - nginx routes /api/v3/... collection endpoints to the UI SPA, so they answer 404 with HTML. Use the ORM shell instead:

sudo podman exec -it authentik-server ak shell

Real admins are in the Infra group. The old akadmin account is disabled.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
Status 2026-11-16: probably not running. Nothing serves dashboard.int.leighhack.org any more - the name isn't in the router's DNS table and doesn't resolve - and no device has had a lease under that name. The AIO PC may still be sitting in the main space, but the DashKiosk instance this page manages is not reachable. Check with infra before spending time on it.

The dashboard is a AIO (all-in-one) PC that shows interesting stuff about the hackspace, either the current status, flyers for upcoming events or just fun bits of information.

docs.title: System
docs.text:
The system is a

  • Intel Atom J1900
  • 8GB RAM
  • 32GB eMMC
  • RTL WiFi card

docs.title: Software
docs.text: Currently it has Ubuntu 22, and has a very bare bones configuration, making use of snaps for the display framework.

docs.title: Ubuntu Frame
docs.text:
Ubuntu Frame is a snap package that provide a Wayland environment for other snaps and applications.

# snap install ubuntu-frame
# snap install ubuntu-frame-vnc

docs.title: Display configuration
docs.text: As we have the display rotated 90 degrees it requires a small tweak to the config of Ubuntu Frame.

docs.title: WPE Webkit Mir Kiosk
docs.text:
A snap that bundles together a simline Webkit browser with some very basic configuration options. All it needs is connection to a Wayland environment and the URL to load.

# snap install wpe-webkit-mir-kiosk
# snap connect wpe-webkit-mir-kiosk ubuntu-frame:wayland
# snap connect wpe-webkit-mir-kiosk:system-observe
# snap set wpe-webkit-mir-kiosk url=http://localhost:9400/receiver

docs.title: DashKiosk
docs.text:
Management interface

# snap install dashkiosk

docs.title: Gateway / Router
docs.text:
Our router is a NixOS box called gw, at 10.3.1.1 on VLAN 225. It took over from the pfSense box on 2026-10-21, and the appliance is retired. There is no web UI: it is configured from the infrastructure repo (machines/gw/), deployed with a NixOS switch, and reached over ssh.

Hardware is a Supermicro X9SCM (Xeon E3-1220 v2, 8 GB), two Intel NICs - router-lan carrying the VLAN trunk to Switch 1, router-uplink to the AAISP hub.

docs.title: What Lives On It
docs.text:
Thing What it does dnsmasq DNS for int.leighhack.org, DHCP and router advertisements for every VLAN nftables The firewall and NAT, generated from common/config.nix's LOCAL_NETWORK table xl2tpd The AAISP L2TP tunnel, which is ppp0 and is the network's real uplink wan-manager Finds every other uplink (USB tether, any Wi-Fi adapter), ranks them, repairs routes nginx The front door: TLS, every vhost, nginx-sso, and anubis headscale + headplane The tailnet control server, and its admin UI network-status network-info.int.leighhack.org - live uplink, interface, connection and lease tables NUT + ups-watchdog The UPS on its USB port, the outage countdown, and the ordered shutdown of the fleet

machines/gw/README.md in the repo is the authority on all of it, including the four commands that prove the router is doing its job.

docs.text:
The mill provides internet access via a gigabit internal network. It can be a bit unreliable but it works for our general usage.

  • ISP: Awareness Software Ltd (AS34931)
  • Mill Network Administrator: Mark Nightingale, Image Village.

Access to the mill network is provided by a singular CAT5 delivered to the rear of the main space, just above where Rack1 is.

docs.title: Hackspace Connectivity
docs.text:
Our internet connection uses the mill's shared network, but we have a Business L2TP 'VPN' to Andrew Arnold, who provide us with 600Mb/sec, 10TB/month, and a /29 block of IPv4 and a /48 IPv6.

  • Line ID: lhc1@a
  • Account ID: A8***0A
  • Control Panel Login: https://control.aa.net.uk/
  • Billing Login: https://accounts.aa.net.uk/

The tunnel is ppp0; if it is down there is no IPv6 and VLAN 225 has no route out. The L2TP connection is currently paid for and managed by Andrew Williams. If you have any queries regarding the connection please contact them.

Egress is split by VLAN: VLAN 225's IPv4 leaves through the tunnel, every other VLAN's IPv4 goes straight out of the hub with a second NAT, and all IPv6 on every VLAN leaves through the tunnel.

docs.title: Backup Uplink
docs.text: wan-manager discovers any second uplink it can - a USB tethered phone, a USB Ethernet adapter, or any Wi-Fi adapter - scans for Leighhack WAN Backup, and measures each candidate's path before selecting it. A selected uplink whose gateway goes quiet is dropped and the routes move. It is IPv4 only: a backup uplink cannot give us IPv6 or inbound connections, because those come with the AAISP tunnel.

docs.title: The Front Door
docs.text:
GW is the only box with a certificate and the only box with a public listener, so it is the only way in from outside. It terminates TLS for every name we run, proxies to the service behind it, and applies the gate:

  • one wildcard ACME certificate, covering leighhack.org, *.leighhack.org, *.ai.leighhack.org, and *.int.leighhack.org
  • every name is one row in common/front-door.nix; the router's nginx is rendered from that table, and common/int-dns.nix is the DNS half of the same fact
  • rows marked sso = true go through nginx-sso, so an app gets a trustworthy X-WEBAUTH-USER header for whoever is logged into Authentik
  • public rows are protected from scrapers by anubis
  • *.int names are answered only on the LAN and the tailnet

The services themselves are origins: plain HTTP, no certificate, no gate, and a socket that only the front door is allowed to reach. Adding an acme or an nginx-sso to another box creates a second front door, which is the one thing not to do here.

docs.title: Add a DNS Record, or a Static DHCP Lease
docs.text:
There is no form for this any more, and no need for one - the answer is a commit:

  • A device that keeps an address goes in common/dns-records.nix: its name, its VLAN, its IPv4, and its MAC (or DHCP client ID). That is one reservation and one DNS record, and the router is restarted for it in the same deploy.
  • A *.int.leighhack.org name is a row in common/int-dns.nix, saying whether the front door answers it, whether the front door serves it, or whether it is dialled as a socket by one box.
  • A new vhost needs a row in common/front-door.nix as well. Two evaluation-time checks refuse a half-move, so a name and its vhost cannot drift apart.

Deploy with just deploy gw from any flake machine (it ssh's in, fetches, switches, and confirms), or just switch while ssh'd to the router.

docs.title: Restart the L2TP Connection
docs.text:
• ssh leigh-admin@10.3.1.1, then sudo -i (root's ssh is not enabled, the admin account has sudo).
  • systemctl status xl2tpd-aaisp.service - it is a never-give-up service, so it should be active and restarting rather than failed.
  • sudo systemctl restart xl2tpd-aaisp.service to redial.
  • ip addr show ppp0 should show an address in 81.187.0.0/16, and network-info's Uplink tab should show the tunnel as the selected uplink with a measured internet path.

docs.title: Check the Network Is Being Routed
docs.text:
The same four checks the cutover was accepted with, on the box:

ip -4 addr show scope global                  # .1 on 225, 226, 227 and 222
getent hosts gw                               # 10.3.1.1
systemctl is-active dnsmasq xl2tpd-aaisp nginx wan-manager
ip route get 1.1.1.1                          # dev ppp0 unless a backup is selected

docs.title: Fix a Camera or Printer That Won't Come Back
docs.text: Don't. A thingino camera's only path back to the network is the Wi-Fi association you'd be changing, so never re-associate a camera over ssh. Ask infra.

docs.title: Do Not
docs.text:
• Do not edit /etc/dnsmasq.d/network.conf (or /etc/dnsmasq-int-vhosts.hosts). Both are generated store paths, and the next deploy silently replaces whatever you wrote.
  • Do not build on the router. It delegates every build to aibox and runs with max-jobs = 0; it is also the box every other box resolves names through.
  • Do not open a service's port to the LAN because the front door is inconvenient. The door and its ACLs are the boundary; a service listening on a LAN address is one that anyone on the network can talk to directly.
  • Do not reboot it to fix something. A reboot takes the network's DNS, DHCP and route away from everything, and the only way back in is the console.

docs.title: Kubernetes Lab (retired)
docs.text:
We ran a small lab cluster: three VMs on the Proxmox host (k8s-lab-01 - k8s-lab-03, 10.3.1.32 - 10.3.1.34), Kubernetes v1.27, single sign-on through id.leighhack.org, and NFS-backed persistent volumes. The plan was MetalLB for LoadBalancer services and Traefik for *.lab.leighhack.org; that never happened.

It is not running, and hasn't been for a while. The VMs are stopped on monster1 (their disks are still on the NAS), k8s-lab.int.leighhack.org no longer resolves, and 10.3.1.32 is aibox now. This page is kept so the design isn't lost, not because anything in it works.

The manifests and per-member namespace setup lived in leigh-hackspace/k8s-lab; the old kubeconfig and kubelogin instructions are in the git history of this page.

If you want the cluster back, the honest starting point is "build a new one and delete these VMs" - three 8 GB nodes is most of what the host has, and a 2023 v1.27 cluster has no upgrade path anyone here has tested. Talk to infra before claiming those addresses again.

docs.title: NAS
docs.text:
One box does storage: nas2.int.leighhack.org (10.3.1.6), an HP MicroServer Gen8 running TrueNAS. It keeps the camera recordings, the filestore share, every Proxmox VM disk, the backups, and member home directories, so anything that matters to the space is somewhere in here.

  • Web UI: truenas.int.leighhack.org (through the front door, Infra only)
  • One ZFS pool, sas-10k, about 14.5 TiB
  • Everything on it is out-of-flake: the appliance is configured in its own UI, and the infra repo only declares the mounts on the boxes that use it

docs.title: What's On It
docs.text:
Dataset NFS export Used by cameras yes Frigate's recordings filestore yes, and over SMB The Filestore share backups yes The borg repositories from the fleet proxmox-monster-ds1 yes Every Proxmox VM disk, over nas2-nfs ds-home, home yes Member home directories ds-photos yes Photo storage retrogames yes The retro machine's ROMs ix-applications no TrueNAS's own apps directory, nothing of ours

The exports are locked to 10.3.1.0/24 except filestore, ds-photos and ds-home.

Member homes are the one thing here with per-person permissions on them: the ACL is your Authentik account, and the uid it maps to is derived from your Authentik user id. Which means the account isn't just how you log in, it's how your files know you.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text: There is no second NAS and no replication, so treat the pool as the single copy. It is also slow to come up after a power cut, and that is a fact about the whole fleet rather than an inconvenience: every box that mounts it waits for it forever rather than failing (wait-for-nas.service), and Proxmox refuses to start any VM until the export answers. If the network is back and the services aren't, this is usually why.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
services1 pushes its /srv - the databases and state behind most of what Internal Services lists - to a borg repository over SSH on a schedule. The borg server is a container (borg-server, an Incus container on the NAS) listening on port 3022:

borg list ssh://backups@nas2.int.leighhack.org:3022/backups/services1.int.leighhack.org/borg/srv

A few honest caveats: the backups live on the same box as the data, nothing is copied off site, and nobody has verified a restore recently. If you have something genuinely irreplaceable, keep a second copy of it yourself.

docs.title: The Old QNAP (retired)
docs.text:
The QNAP TS-431+ at 10.3.1.5 (nas1) is off. Its address is still reserved and its name still resolves, which is why it looks like it might be up; it does not answer ping, and the nas1-nfs Proxmox datastore that used to point at it is disabled.

It went away because of storage, not because of failure: a single 4-bay box couldn't hold the camera recordings and the VM disks both. Its Samba service was the thing that couldn't talk to Authentik's LDAP, which is why SMB was disabled on it - on TrueNAS, SMB just works, and the guest shares are served from there.

docs.title: Check Disk Health
docs.text:
• Login to truenas.int.leighhack.org as an Infra member.
  • Pool status is on the dashboard; per-disk SMART results are under Storage → Disks.
  • From a terminal, ssh leigh-admin@10.3.1.6 then sudo zpool status sas-10k - a pool in DEGRADED here is the moment to ask infra, not the moment to keep working.

docs.title: Add a Share
docs.text:
• In the TrueNAS UI, create or pick the dataset, then add the NFS or SMB share you want.
  • If a machine in the fleet needs it as a mount, that half is a commit: add an entry to that machine's infra.nas.exports list (machines/<box>/hardware-configuration.nix) and deploy. Mounts and their automounts are generated from that one list, so the two halves can't drift.

docs.title: Don't
docs.text:
• Don't edit /etc/sudoers on the NAS. Middleware regenerates it at boot and the generated file has no #includedir, so a hand edit or a drop-in is simply lost. The passwordless sudo for leigh-admin is set as the middleware user record - do it that way, through the API or the UI.
  • Don't move or rename a dataset that Proxmox or a mount is using without taking the consumer off it first; the automounts retry forever, which reads as a hung machine rather than a missing path.

docs.title: Network Switches
docs.text:
Three managed switches, all HP ProCurve, all configured over Telnet only - there is no API and no web UI on the devices themselves:

Name Model Address Firmware switch1 HP ProCurve 2510G-48 (J9280A) 10.3.1.2 Y.11.44 switch2 HP ProCurve 2510G-48 (J9280A) 10.3.1.3 Y.11.44 switch3 HP ProCurve 2824 (J4903A) 10.3.1.4 I.10.107

switch1 is the core: the router's trunk lands on it, and it carries every VLAN. switch2 feeds the Pi Room, Classroom and Social Space, and switch3 the fabrication area. While the 2824 is the older switch it offers L3-lite capabilities that we don't use; the others are plain managed L2 switches. All three speak the standard HP CLI.

  • CLI Reference for the 2510 series
  • CLI Reference for the 2800 series

docs.title: The Web UI
docs.text:
switch.int.leighhack.org is the supported way to change a port. It signs in with your Authentik account (Infra group), polls all three switches every minute into a shadow copy, shows you a diff, and applies a queued batch on the switch box - then follows every batch it applied with write memory, because these switches hold a change in RAM until something saves it.

Use it in preference to a telnet session. A hand-made change is invisible to it until the next poll, and is undone by a reboot: a mains blip on 2026-10-31 reverted a day of hand edits on all three switches.

docs.title: Logging In
docs.text:
telnet 10.3.1.2, username agent, password in the password manager. agent is a Manager, so you get in read-only and have to enable before conf will do anything.

You will see Can't reach RADIUS server. printed on a perfectly successful login. That is this firmware's generic "authentication failed" line: the switches are configured to try RADIUS against Authentik first and fall back to their local account database, and RADIUS never answers - there is no agent user in Authentik, so the outpost sends no reply at all. So your id.leighhack.org account does not work on the switches today, and every login costs a few seconds of RADIUS timeout. switch3 is the slow one: 15-25 s to a prompt is normal there.

Fixing it means giving Authentik an agent user whose password matches the switches' local one, or dropping RADIUS from those accounts' auth order; until then a login_failed for agent in Authentik is this, and not an incident.

docs.title: Enabling a port untagged on a VLAN
docs.text:
• Login to the switch via telnet, and run enable.
  • Run conf
  • Switch to the VLAN context needed with vlan 225
  • Type untagged 25 representing the port number, ranges can be specified e.g. 25-30
  • exit, exit, wr mem

docs.title: Enabling a trunk port on multiple VLANs
docs.text: • Same as a untagged port, switch to each VLAN and use tagged <portid> rather than untagged

docs.title: Reading what a port is in
docs.text: show vlan <id> leaves the Name column blank for dynamically-learned members, and show port name doesn't exist on this firmware, so port names come from show running-config. switch-gui merges the six show commands needed to describe a port; doing it by hand means running all six.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text: Nothing saves itself. running-config is in RAM and startup-config is what loads at boot, so a change made by hand is only real once you've typed write memory. A reboot is the only undo for a bad change, and for a change made at a console it's also the only way back - so check what you've written before you save, and don't save the thing you were only testing.

docs.title: Proxmox
docs.text:
There is one Proxmox host, monster1 (10.3.1.11), running Proxmox VE 9.x. The UI is at monster.int.leighhack.org - sign in with your Authentik account (the leighhack.org OpenID realm).

It is called "monster" after a machine that no longer exists: the HP SL2x170z blades and monster2-monster5 are gone, and what's running now is a single desktop box.

Machine HP 290 G1 SFF CPU / RAM Intel i5-8500 (6 cores) / 32 GB Local disk 500 GB SSD Not in this flake Nothing about this host or its VMs is declarative

There is no cluster, and no redundancy. HA is enabled, but with one node that means "restart a VM that dies", not "fail over".

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
VM disks are qcow2 files on the NAS over NFS: nas2-nfs is 10.3.1.6:/mnt/sas-10k/proxmox-monster-ds1, mounted at /mnt/pve/nas2-nfs. The second mount (nas1-nfs, the old QNAP) is disabled.

Two consequences that bite people:

  • After a power cut, every VM start fails with storage 'nas2-nfs' is not online while the NAS is still booting. Check pvesm status and mount | grep nas2-nfs before blaming a VM; the fix is to wait and retry.
  • Boots take minutes even when nothing is wrong, because every disk is a file on a network share with cache=direct.

There are no backup jobs and no snapshots on this host. /etc/pve/jobs.cfg is empty, and the NAS holds the only copy of every disk image. Treat anything you put here as dispensable unless you have copied it somewhere else.

docs.text:
VMID Name Address State 109 apps1 10.3.1.30 Running. Mostly superseded by services1, but a few things still live in it 127 web1 10.3.1.39 Running. The hackspace website: webhooks., web-test. and retro.leighhack.org 108 authentik 10.3.1.36 Stopped on purpose since the 2026-10-28 cutover to containers on services1. It must stay stopped 128 mercury 10.3.1.166 Stopped. The intercom, replaced by Asterisk on services1 107 mx1 - Stopped since 2026-10. This was the outbound mail relay 100/103/104 k8s-lab-* - Stopped, see Kubernetes Lab 110-118 GOAD / Windows lab - Stopped since 2023-2025 132 Terraria - Stopped

Anything not in that list is dormant disk. Before starting a VM to "check whether anyone is using it", ask in Slack - half of these have last written to disk years ago.

10.3.1.36 is answered by services1 now, but its DHCP reservation is still live and still names the old VM's MAC - booting VM 108 takes that address back, and two hosts answering one address is silent for whoever is trying to log in. The intercom's address is protected the other way: the router is told dhcp-host=10.3.1.166,ignore so nothing else can be handed it.

docs.title: Allowing users access to the Cluster
docs.text:
• Login to https://monster.int.leighhack.org/ as a Infra member.
  • Click on 'Datacenter (monster)' in the left menu.
  • Goto Users and find the user that requires access.
  • Either add them to the 'Infra', or 'Members' group as needed.

docs.title: Login without using id.leighhack.org/Authentik
docs.text:
• Go to https://monster.int.leighhack.org/
  • On the login screen, select the dropdown and pick 'Linux PAM'
  • Username is 'root', password is in the password manager.

docs.title: Starting a VM that HA manages
docs.text:
Use ha-manager, never qm start, or HA and the VM disagree about who owns it:

ha-manager set vm:109 --state started

If the service is sitting in error, clearing it is disable, wait, then start - doing both in one loop races and the start is rejected:

ha-manager disable vm:109 ; sleep 15 ; ha-manager enable vm:109 ; ha-manager set vm:109 --state started

The VMs that are not HA-managed (107 mx1, 132 Terraria) are qm started by hand.

docs.title: After an outage
docs.text: docs/monster-powercut-runbook.md in the infra repo is the full procedure, including what to start in which order and how long the NAS takes. The host is deliberately not on the router's shutdown list, so it stays up until the mains actually go.

docs.title: Hackspace State Switch v1
docs.text:
The state switch is a physical switch located near the Main Space entrance doors. This small device provide a physical open/close indicator for the hackspace, and the status is made available via the Space API endpoint, Home Assistand, Slack bot, and website.

The device itself is a simple ESP8266 (A WeMoS D1-Mini clone with USB-C) with a RGB LED, and a rocker switch. It runs ESPHome and connects to our Home Assistant instance, which lives on services1 and is at ha.int.leighhack.org.

It answers to big-button on the wireless VLAN (10.3.2.21). The switch drives the open/closed state in Home Assistant, and that one boolean is what api.leighhack.org's state.open, the Slack bot, and the status page all read - there is no other source of whether we're open.

docs.title: Physical
docs.text:
• RGB LED is wired to D5, D6, D7, and controlled via PWM
  • Switch is connected to D4

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
Due to not reading the docs before fitting together, the switch is connected to D4, which is needed to be pulled high at boot, so if the switch is left in the "on" state, the device will not boot.

Label GPIO Input Output Notes D0 GPIO16 no interrupt no PWM or I2C support HIGH at boot used to wake up from deep sleep D1 GPIO5 OK OK often used as SCL (I2C) D2 GPIO4 OK OK often used as SDA (I2C) D3 GPIO0 pulled up OK connected to FLASH button, boot fails if pulled LOW D4 GPIO2 pulled up OK HIGH at boot connected to on-board LED, boot fails if pulled LOW D5 GPIO14 OK OK SPI (SCLK) D6 GPIO12 OK OK SPI (MISO) D7 GPIO13 OK OK SPI (MOSI) D8 GPIO15 pulled to GND OK SPI (CS) Boot fails if pulled HIGH RX GPIO3 OK RX pin HIGH at boot TX GPIO1 TX pin OK HIGH at boot debug output at boot, boot fails if pulled LOW A0 ADC0 Analog Input X

docs.title: Source
docs.text: The Hackspace State Switch uses ESPHome. Its config was kept in the esphome-config repository in the Leigh Hackspace GitHub org, alongside the other ESPHome devices; that repository isn't public any more, so the current YAML is with infra.

docs.title: Code of Conduct
docs.text:
Leigh Hackspace is a shared community workspace that offers the facilities needed to make a variety of projects for locals that don’t have the accessibility at home. We provide inspiration, equipment, ideas, support, training and even some materials for ‘hacking’. All with a great community spirit and a ‘can-do’ atmosphere.

We have a few ground rules that we ask people to adhere to. This code applies equally to members, volunteers and guests.

This isn't an exhaustive list of things that you can or can't do. Rather, take it in the spirit in which it's intended - a guide to make it easier to enrich all of us, our projects, and the broader communities in which we participate.

This code of conduct applies to all spaces managed by Leigh Hackspace. This includes, but not limited to, Leigh Spinner Mill, social platforms, events, mailing lists and any other forums created by the project team which the community uses for communication. In addition, violations of this code outside these spaces may affect a person's ability to participate within them.

  • Be friendly and patient.
  • Be kind
  • Be welcoming. We strive to be a community that welcomes and supports people of all backgrounds and identities. This includes, but is not limited to, members of any race, ethnicity, culture, national origin, colour, immigration status, social and economic class, educational level, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, age, size, family status, political belief, religion, and mental or physical ability.
  • Be considerate. You will be working in a communal space, and you in turn will be responsible for cleaning up after yourself. This includes storage of projects within the Hackspace. Projects must be stored within the dedicated spaces. If left out, Hackspace holds the right to relocate projects to an area where they are not in the way of others.
  • Be respectful. Not all of us will agree all the time, but disagreement is no excuse for poor behaviour and poor manners. We might all experience some frustration now and then, but we cannot allow that frustration to turn into a personal attack. It's important to remember that a community where people feel uncomfortable or threatened is not a productive one. Members of the community should be respectful when dealing with other members as well as with people outside the community.
  • Be careful in the words that you choose. Be kind to others. Do not insult or put down other participants. Harassment and other exclusionary behaviour aren't acceptable. This includes, but is not limited to:
  • Violent threats or language directed against another person.
  • Discriminatory jokes and language.
  • Posting sexually explicit or violent material.
  • Posting (or threatening to post) other people's personally identifying information ("doxing").
  • Personal insults, especially those using racist or sexist terms.
  • Unwelcome sexual attention.
  • Advocating for, or encouraging, any of the above behavior.
  • Repeated harassment of others. In general, if someone asks you to stop, then stop.
  • When we disagree, try to understand why. Disagreements, both social and technical, happen all the time and the Hackspace community is no exception. It is important that we resolve disagreements and differing views constructively. A strength of Hackspace is the varied community, people from a wide range of backgrounds. Different people have different perspectives on issues. Being unable to understand why someone holds a viewpoint doesn't mean that they're wrong. Don't forget that it is human to err and blaming each other doesn't get us anywhere. Instead, focus on helping to resolve issues and learning from mistakes.

See the GNU Kind Communications Guidelines for more guidance on constructive interactions.

If you believe someone is violating the code of conduct, we ask that you report it by emailing info@leighack.org.

Leigh Hackspace is a community built on respect, collaboration, and mutual understanding. We believe that everyone has the right to work in a positive and supportive environment. In the event of a dispute, we encourage open dialogue and peaceful resolution. However, we understand that conflicts can sometimes escalate and need formal intervention.

In such cases, disputes will be handled directly by the Leigh Hackspace directors. They will take an unbiased and careful approach to understand the situation, speak to all parties involved, and find a fair resolution. The directors have the community's best interests at heart and will always strive to maintain a positive and productive environment for everyone.

If you're facing a dispute, don't hesitate to reach out. Our directors are here to help and ensure that Leigh Hackspace remains a welcoming and harmonious place for all its members.

docs.title: In-built screen is blank after booting a Linux kernel
docs.text:
Issue tracker

This is due to the modeset being wrong for the display (the values provided by the VBIOS seem to be wrong). To disable modesetting at boot add the following to the kernel command line:

i915.modeset=0

This will disable the iGPU for use in X/Wayland, so useful for getting to the installer of some distributions.

docs.title: The screen is not rotated correctly in Linux on boot
docs.text:
As root:

echo 1 > /sys/class/graphics/fbcon/rotate_all

X/Wayland can be done with Xrandr

docs.title: The sensor keeps rotating the screen incorrectly.
docs.text:
This issue is due to the 'IIO' sensors not being mapped correctly within Linux. This sensor works perfectly fine in Windows with the correct driver, but Linux doesn't seem to be able to detect the screen rotated. The rotation will work if the screen is rotated outwards like a tablet, but normally it believes that the correct rotation in laptop mode is 'right_up'.

A couple of services are used in this system.

  • udev
  • systemd-hwdb
  • iio-sensor-proxy

First you need to create a rule for the sensor device in the hwdb, /etc/udev/hwdb.d/60-sensors.hwdb:

# A wide matching rule, but the Koosmile P8 has no Manf/Prod strings
# This fixes the screen in 'laptop' mode to rotate correctly, but not tablet mode
sensor:modalias:acpi:BOSC0200*
  ACCEL_MOUNT_MATRIX=-1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1

This file will set a udev variable for the device of ACCEL_MOUNT_MATRIX, which iio-sensor-proxy uses. Then you need to reload the hardware DB, and get udev to 'trigger' for the sensor device, recreating the settings and variables for it.

# systemd-hwdb update
# udevadm trigger -v -p DEVNAME=/dev/iio:device0

Next, you need to restart iio-sensor-proxy

# systemd restart iio-sensor-proxy

Depending on your desktop environment, you may need to do some further configuration or install a library, in the case of GNOME you'll need the Screen Rotate extension.
